t: LeetCode 2156 — Find Substring With Given Hash Value
o: hash(sub, power, modulo) treats a length-k substring as a base-power number whose digits are val("a")=1 through val("z")=26, reduced modulo m. We must return the earliest window of length k whose hash equals hashValue; the tests guarantee one exists. In Example 1, hash("ee") = (5 + 35) mod 20 = 0 and no earlier window qualifies. In Example 2 both "fbx" and "bxz" hash to 32 under power 31 and modulo 100, but "fbx" starts first and must be returned. The string can reach 2*10^4 with k up to its length, so evaluating every window from scratch (up to ~4*10^8 multiply-adds) is risky, while a sliding-window hash updates each window in O(1). Beware: modulo is arbitrary — not necessarily prime and allowed to share factors with power — and values reach 10^9, so 64-bit arithmetic (BigInt in JavaScript) is required.
k: Slide windows right-to-left via H_i = ((H_(i+1) - val(s[i+k])*p^(k-1)) * p + val(s[i])) mod m — O(1) per step with no modular inverse needed.
Record every match while sweeping right-to-left; the final recorded start is automatically the leftmost, i.e., the first substring.
power and modulo may share factors, so inverse-based sliding is invalid, and products approaching 10^18 need 64-bit/BigInt precision.

a.n: Approach 1: Evaluate every window from scratch
a.i: Compute hash(sub, power, modulo) independently for each length-k window, exactly as the formula reads. With n and k up to 2*10^4 this can reach ~4*10^8 digit operations, which times out in slower languages, but it is the obvious starting point and a perfect reference implementation for validating the rolling version.
s: Precompute powers p^0 .. p^(k-1) reduced modulo m.
For each start i, accumulate val * p^j over the k characters, reducing modulo m.
Return the substring immediately on the first match.
a.t: O(n*k) — every window is re-evaluated character by character

a.i: Adjacent windows share k-1 characters. Removing the tail contribution val(s[i+k])*p^(k-1), multiplying the remainder by p, and prepending the new head character turns H_(i+1) into H_i in O(1). Sweeping right-to-left makes the popped character the window tail, sidestepping any need for the inverse of power modulo m (which may not exist when gcd(power, modulo) != 1). Because we overwrite the recorded match on every hit, the survivor at the end is the leftmost match.
s: Compute pk = p^(k-1) mod m and the hash of the last window (start n-k) by Horner right-to-left.
Scan starts i from n-k down to 0; whenever h equals hashValue, overwrite the recorded best start.
Slide left: h = (((h - val(s[i+k-1])*pk) mod m + m) mod m * p + val(s[i-1])) mod m.
a.t: O(n) — constant-time roll per window after O(k) setup
a.sp: O(1) — a few accumulators (plus BigInt temporaries in JavaScript)

w: Derive the left-slide recurrence on paper and test it on Example 1 before coding. Classic bugs: negative residues after the subtraction (fix with ((x % m) + m) % m), popping s[i+k] instead of s[i+k-1], and attempting a left-to-right slide using an inverse of p that does not exist when gcd(p, m) != 1. In JavaScript, use BigInt for the multiply-back step since intermediates approach 10^18, beyond the exact range of doubles. Follow-ups: return all matching windows, adapt to classic Rabin-Karp search, or support streaming input.
